title: Don’t scare off investors, Padilla tells protesters ‘demonizing’ AI
summary: Senator Robin Padilla wants the Philippines to get a slice of the trillion-dollar AI pie, protests be damned

blocks.text: MINORITY. Senator Robin Padilla wants the Philippines to get a slice of the trillion-dollar AI pie, protests be damned

items: Senator Robin Padilla criticized the growing opposition to artificial intelligence (AI) in the Philippines, urging the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) to support AI investments.
Padilla highlighted protests against AI during the ASEAN Summit, expressing concern that Filipinos might miss out on significant economic opportunities in the AI sector.

Senator Robin Padilla has a bone to pick with Filipinos “demonizing” artificial intelligence (AI), and he wants the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) on his side.

During a Senate session on Tuesday, November 24, Padilla took several minutes of BSP Governor Eli Remolona’s time to lament what he saw as the growing opposition to AI in the Philippines, an industry worth trillions of dollars that Filipinos, he argued, would be foolish to pass up.
Throughout his impassioned defense of AI investments, the senator was careful not to utter two words: Pax Silica. Neither did he name any of the would-be investors.
But he did make clear the target of his ire.

“Ito pong nakaraang ASEAN, napansin ‘nyo po ba, mahal naming Governor, na ang daming nagpoprotesta, ang daming mga boses, ang daming maiingay ang nagsasabi na huwag natin papasukin ang AI,” Padilla said.
(During this past ASEAN, did you notice, dear Governor, that there were so many protesters, so many voices, so many noisy people saying we shouldn’t let AI in.)

blocks.caption: Don’t scare off investors, Padilla tells protesters ‘demonizing’ AI

blocks.text: Recall that on the opening day of the ASEAN Summit, November 15, hundreds of protesters were arrested in Muntinlupa City for demonstrating against the US-led Pax Silica initiative and the visit of US President Donald Trump. Some 236 people spent more than 70 hours in detention before being released.

Among the protesters’ concerns were the potential displacement of indigenous communities and farmers, as well as the energy and water requirements of the proposed advanced manufacturing hub in New Clark City, Tarlac. A bill is already pending in the House of Representatives to establish a special economic zone for advanced industries.
The senator isn’t the only one bewildered by the protests. No less than President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said he was “perplexed” by them, insisting that no data centers would be built at the site.
Back in the Senate, Padilla even urged the BSP to release a statement in favor of AI adoption, taking issue with the anti-AI rhetoric he was hearing on the streets, in the news, and on social media.
“Dine-demonize ang AI at parang sinasabi nila na huwag natin itong tanggapin sa bansa natin (They’re demonizing AI, as if telling us not to welcome it into our country),” Padilla said.

The BSP Governor was equally careful with his words. While the central bank chief conceded that the Philippines could risk being left behind in AI investments, Padilla could hardly get him to say anything directly about the protests.
“Hindi po kontrahin. Pag-ingatan lang (Don’t oppose it. Just be careful),” Remolona said of AI, citing its capacity to deceive and hallucinate.
In fact, as the governor pointed out, the BSP already uses AI. It has even issued guidance to banks on adopting the technology while managing its accompanying risks.
Perhaps Padilla would do good to consider what role the Philippines should play in welcoming the AI industry.

Consider how renowned historian Yuval Noah Harari, speaking at Rappler’s Social Good Summit, warned of a “new imperial age” in which control over AI infrastructure could give foreign powers big leverage over smaller nations. Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa likewise warned that the “predatory and extractive” practices of Big Tech are advancing far faster than governments’ ability to regulate them.

blocks.caption: At Rappler summit, human rights figures call for solidarity amid AI threats

blocks.text: But for all the concerns and nuances that should come with any debate on AI’s economic potential, Padilla seemed more struck by an intense fear of missing out.
“Meron pong mga gustong mag-invest dito sa ating bansa na kinokontra ng napakadaming grupo,” the senator said. “Kapag tayo hindi kumuha ng piece of pie diyan, eh kawawa naman na tayong mga Pilipino.”
(We have people who want to invest in our country who are being opposed by so many groups. If we don’t get a piece of that pie, we Filipinos will again be pitiful.) – Rappler.com
